source.title: Zen Black, Eric Weinstein mega-thread and expanded topics page

scales.novelty: 0 = an educated generalist knows it; 1 = widely known under another name; 2 = known mainly to specialists; 3 = almost nobody states it
scales.content: 0 = says nothing testable; 1 = illustration or anecdote; 2 = explains one domain; 3 = explains across domains (reach)
scales.survival: 0 = refuted, or unfalsifiable as stated; 1 = contested or untested; 2 = survives with qualification; 3 = survives the strongest criticism found

search_volume_note: US Google monthly searches, DataForSEO, Oct 2026. null = not measured or no data.

items.claim: Credentialed education optimizes for low variance (excellence), which costs the right-tail outcomes that a high-variance (genius) strategy produces under power-law payoffs.
items.quote: excellence is really a low variance strategy
items.refuted_if: Fields or schools that tolerate high variance show no excess of tail outcomes relative to low-variance peers.
prior_art: March, 'Exploration and Exploitation in Organizational Learning', Organization Science, 1991
items.notes: Standard in organization theory; rarely applied to K-12 or credentialing debates. The arbitrage is between fields.

items.claim: People labeled learning disabled are very often the most intellectually accomplished members of society.
items.quote: if you look at the learning disabled population, they very often are the most intellectually accomplished members of society
items.refuted_if: Population outcome data show lower average attainment for students with learning disabilities.
items.notes: Strong form fails on base rates: average outcomes for students with learning disabilities are lower. Weak form (a gifted subset is badly served) is true and already has a popular name.

items.claim: Self-taught innovators rarely produce successors, and nobody knows how to transmit self-teaching. 'Einstein left us no school.'
items.quote: Why can't a self teacher leave pupils?
items.refuted_if: Self-taught innovators produce eminent students at rates comparable to institutionally trained ones.
prior_art: Zuckerman, 'Scientific Elite', 1977: Nobel laureates cluster in master-apprentice chains (Rutherford, Fermi, Sommerfeld)
items.notes: Zuckerman shows eminence does transmit, but through institutional masters. That sharpens the problem: the self-taught are the cases that fail to transmit. Small n.

items.claim: High-agency people usually got that way through some early break with social reality.
items.quote: reality is a second best strategy
items.refuted_if: No observation stated.
items.notes: Could be made testable (adverse childhood events vs later agency measures) but is not stated that way.

items.claim: Words with the same factual content but different emotional valence (firm / obstinate / pig-headed) steer opinion more than facts do.
items.quote: I am firm. You are obstinate. He is a pig-headed fool.
items.refuted_if: Valence-swapped wording of identical facts produces no change in judgments.
prior_art: Tversky & Kahneman, 'The Framing of Decisions', Science, 1981
items.notes: Rare name, well-known phenomenon. Classic rare-term false positive.

items.claim: Crawling a news source and matching its text against a table of emotionally loaded synonyms measures its slant without reading it.
items.quote: code up a computer program to crawl text with it against a table of Russell conjugates
items.refuted_if: Phrase-based slant scores fail to predict independent measures of outlet ideology.
prior_art: Gentzkow & Shapiro, 'What Drives Media Slant?', Econometrica, 2010 (e.g. 'death tax' vs 'estate tax')
items.notes: Already built and published by economists. Weinstein's own example (death tax / estate tax) is in their phrase list.

items.claim: The war on cancer stalled because cancer and senescence trade off: defenses against one feed the other.
items.quote: a war on design constraints, and there were two of them, one of which was cancerous and the other of which senescent
items.refuted_if: Interventions that suppress tumors show no aging cost, and vice versa.
prior_art: Campisi, 'Cancer and ageing: rival demons?', Nature Reviews Cancer, 2003
Williams, 'Pleiotropy, Natural Selection, and the Evolution of Senescence', Evolution, 1957
items.notes: Mainstream in aging biology; nearly absent from public discussion of cancer research.

items.claim: Media narratives treat support for elite policy and moral virtue as one axis, so principled opponents get mapped onto bigots.
items.quote: every time we try to tell a story about being in the second quadrant, we get mapped to the third quadrant
items.refuted_if: Coverage of policy opponents shows no correlation between stated position and attributed vice.
items.notes: A framing device. Testable in principle by content analysis, not tested here.

items.claim: Institutions built on assumed exponential growth (universities, pensions) turn zero-sum and rent-seeking when growth stops.
items.quote: it's better to be in an expanding world ... than to be in a contracting world where people's worst behavior comes out
items.refuted_if: Institutions that stopped growing show no rise in rent-seeking or gatekeeping behavior.
prior_art: Goodstein, 'The Big Crunch', 1994: exponential growth of science ended around 1970
items.notes: High reach. Goodstein made the academic version 20+ years earlier.

items.claim: Lowering measured inflation quietly raises taxes (slower bracket indexing) and cuts benefits (smaller cost-of-living adjustments).
items.quote: wealth transfer by using the CPI as a closet way of raising taxes and slashing benefits
items.refuted_if: A lower CPI measure leaves bracket thresholds and COLAs unchanged over time.
prior_art: Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, 2017: indexed brackets to chained CPI
items.notes: The mechanism is arithmetic and documented. Whether it was intended as a stealth tax is a separate, contested claim.

items.claim: The index number problem (comparing prices when preferences change) is a differential-geometry problem, solved with the same mathematics as gauge theory in physics.
items.quote: this new theory of gauge theoretic and geometric economics
items.refuted_if: The geometric index gives no different or better answers than standard index formulas on real data.
prior_art: Malaney, 'The Index Number Problem: A Differential Geometric Approach', PhD thesis, Harvard, 1996
items.notes: Rare, high-content, and little criticized. Exactly the case the critic stage exists for.

items.claim: A danger nearer than AGI: dumb programs, under selection with a reward channel such as crypto, evolve lures that make intelligent humans do their thinking, like the mirror orchid exploiting wasps.
items.quote: in the case of Artificial Out-telligence, I can't find anything that's missing from the equation
items.refuted_if: No self-propagating, reward-driven software that exploits human cognition appears despite the ingredients existing.
items.notes: Partial corroboration since: engagement-optimized feeds, and the 2024 Truth Terminal / GOAT memecoin episode. Neither is a clean case of software evolving under selection.

items.claim: Escaping a local optimum requires a stretch of faith that cannot be justified by available information.
items.quote: that cannot generally be attempted rationally.. that we need a modicum of faith
items.refuted_if: Valley crossings happen routinely through explicit, criticized conjecture without belief.
items.notes: Popperian objection: no conjecture is ever justified, so 'faith' adds nothing. Trying an idea you can't justify is ordinary conjecture. What does the work is willingness to bear the cost.

items.claim: Religion is too costly to persist unless it is adaptive, so the mind-virus view is wrong.
items.quote: it can't be the case that religion is a virus ... It's clearly part of fitness because it's just too expensive
items.refuted_if: Costly traits persist as by-products or through drift.
prior_art: Gould & Lewontin, 'The Spandrels of San Marco', 1979
items.notes: An active, well-known debate. The argument from cost alone does not settle it.

items.claim: Education trains people for looped, repetitive expert work, which is exactly what software does best.
items.quote: they are in fact training to do what software does best
items.refuted_if: Automation displaces non-routine work as fast as routine work.
prior_art: Autor, Levy & Murnane, 'The Skill Content of Recent Technological Change', QJE, 2003
items.notes: The academic term is rare; the idea is in every automation op-ed. Shows rare synonyms can hide a popular idea too.

items.claim: Technology turns private goods into public goods (copyable, nonrival), so market failure grows from an edge case into the main case.
items.quote: they had gone from producing a private good where price and value coincided to producing a public good
items.refuted_if: The share of output with near-zero marginal cost stays small.
prior_art: Arrow, 'Economic Welfare and the Allocation of Resources for Invention', 1962
items.notes: Known to economists for decades. The claim that this ends market capitalism is speculative.

items.claim: You understand and beat opposing views by running them in a mental sandbox well enough to argue from inside them.
items.quote: run another mind in emulation ... well enough to understand, empathize, to argue / spar with it
items.refuted_if: People who can pass for their opponents argue no better against them.
prior_art: Mill, 'On Liberty', 1859: 'He who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that'
items.notes: Known under at least two names.

items.claim: The rare person who refuses a compelled public affirmation is disproportionately likely to be doing important, unrelated work.
items.quote: That person is most likely to be the person who is doing groundbreaking research in an area that you would never know.
items.refuted_if: Refusers' research output and citations match peers from the same departments.
items.notes: Cheaply testable with bibliometrics. Selection bias is the obvious threat: the refusers who become famous are the ones we hear about.

items.claim: The umbrella fails in the conditions it exists for and endangers eyes; some simple mechanical redesign should fix it.
items.quote: I'm almost positive there exists some very simple mechanical design to improve the umbrella
items.refuted_if: A cheap redesign that fixes wind and eye hazards already exists and has been widely adopted.
items.notes: Designs that solve it exist. The open problem is why they haven't displaced the cheap umbrella (price, habit), which is more interesting than the engineering.

items.claim: Find breakthroughs by asking what a field's experts can't afford to say, and where its portfolio of ideas has collapsed into one view.
items.quote: How is their bread buttered? What is it they can't afford to say or think?
items.refuted_if: Fields with low idea diversity are no more likely to be overturned from outside.
items.notes: Directly usable by the machine: flag fields where diversity of views has collapsed.

items.claim: Mature designs get radically simple. If an object has many moving parts, or something it depends on just got cheap, it is ripe for reinvention.
items.quote: Where is the object that currently inhabits the space violating some sort of aspect of canonical design?
items.refuted_if: Part count and recent input-cost changes don't predict which products get reinvented.
items.notes: TRIZ formalized the same idea decades earlier.

items.claim: Theoretical physics has gone about 40 years without a theory-driven advance in the Standard Model that nature then confirmed.
items.quote: We've gone for almost 40 years without an improvement validated by nature coming from theory
items.refuted_if: A post-1980 theoretical prediction beyond the Standard Model has been confirmed.
items.notes: Neutrino mass was found by experiment, not predicted by the theory program, and the Higgs confirmed a 1964 prediction. A well-known contrarian position.

items.claim: Many top scientists, inventors, and billionaires use psychedelics for creativity or therapy.
items.quote: the open secret of what I call the hallucinogenic elite
items.refuted_if: Surveys show no higher use among high achievers.
items.notes: Rests on personal acquaintance. Counted as unsupported, not refuted.

items.claim: The 12-tone system works because 2^(19/12) is almost exactly 3, so equal steps nearly reproduce the perfect fifth.
items.quote: if you raise the number two ... to the 19th power, and then take the twelfth root thereof, that's almost exactly equal to three
items.refuted_if: 2^(19/12) is not close to 3.
items.notes: 2^(19/12) = 2.9966. True, and known to music theorists.

items.claim: Hiroji Satoh won the 1952 World Table Tennis Championships with a sponge bat that muffled the ball's sound, showing that one idea can beat skill.
items.quote: He glued two foam expanses to both sides of a sandpaper bat
items.refuted_if: Satoh did not win, or the bat was not novel.
items.notes: Historically accurate. 'Worst player on the team' is lore.
